title: Beef just became a credit problem
body_markdown:
USDA now expects beef and veal prices to rise 9.4% this year, more than triple the increase for food overall. Most of the coverage has treated that as a grocery story about what families pay for ground beef.


We feel the angle that matters most for foodservice distribution has been missed. For a distributor, this is a credit story, and most credit managers are not watching the cattle market.


Here is the thing about a margin squeeze: it never stays where it starts. In August, beef and veal prices were 5.9% higher than a year earlier, while prices at restaurants were up 3.4%, and USDA's latest outlook has restaurant prices rising 3.5% for the full year. For a steakhouse, a burger place or a barbecue joint, beef is not one line on the invoice. It is the menu. When their biggest input rises faster than they can raise prices without losing guests, the difference comes out of their margin, and most independent restaurants did not have much margin to begin with.


When an independent operator gets squeezed, the first bill to slide is usually the one owed to the most patient creditor. In foodservice, that is very often the distributor.


This is also not a blip. The Kansas City Fed published an analysis in August explaining why ranchers have not rebuilt their herds, even though cattle prices look attractive. The cattle needed to rebuild cost about double their 20-year average, drought keeps pushing costs up, and disease risk adds another layer of uncertainty. Historically, herds only start growing two to three years after ranchers begin holding back heifers for breeding. The Fed's conclusion is that beef prices will likely stay elevated for some time, and USDA expects another 4.7% increase in 2027. This is a long squeeze, not a short one.


Anyone who grew up around farming knows there are two ways to learn about the weather. You can check the rain gauge, which tells you exactly how much fell. Or you can look at the sky, which tells you what is coming.


The aging report is a rain gauge. It is accurate and useful, and it only tells you about rain that has already fallen. By the time a beef-heavy account shows up at 60 days, the squeeze has been working on that business for months.


The sky is everything your customer service team and your sales reps hear every day. It is the steakhouse that quietly moves from ribeye to chuck, or from a premium brand to a commodity one. It is the owner who never asked about price and now asks every week, and the invoice disputes that start to pile up. It is orders that get smaller or skip a week, and payments that arrive in part instead of in full. None of this shows up in the aging report until it is already a collections problem, and in most distributors the people who see the clouds and the person who reads the rain gauge rarely compare notes.


There is a procurement side to this too. If you have customers on fixed or long-dated beef pricing, someone is carrying the gap between what was quoted and what you are paying now, and it is worth knowing whether that someone is you. This is where independents can be smarter than a national broadliner. You know which customers are on which deals, and you can have a real conversation about what is fair for both sides before the margin quietly disappears.


So what should a distributor do this week? First, pull the list of accounts where beef is a large share of what they buy. That is your watch list. Second, ask customer service and sales to flag mix changes, price complaints and changes in order rhythm on those accounts, and make sure that reaches credit every week, not when the account hits 60 days. Third, check where fixed or long-dated beef pricing leaves you holding the cost. Finally, talk to customers before the invoice does, and bring them options. USDA forecasts pork prices up only 1.2% and poultry up 1% this year, and a menu built partly around them can protect their margin as well as yours.


The bottom line is that some of your customers will struggle through this, and some of the ones who make it will pay others first. The distributor who sees trouble coming, says something early and helps a chef rework a menu is the one who gets paid when money is tight.


Your customers can't stop buying beef. Watch the sky, not just the rain gauge, and make sure you are not the one quietly paying for it. At Burnt, we believe the signals that matter most are already inside your business, and the work is getting them to the right person in time.
